text:
The correct order of total number of atoms present in

(A) 2 moles of cyclohexane

(B) 684 g of sucrose

(C) 90.8 L of dihydrogen at STP

is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let us find the total number of atoms in each case.

We only need to compare, so first calculate the number of moles of atoms in each sample.

(A) 2 moles of cyclohexane
Cyclohexane has formula:

$\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{12}$

So, one molecule of cyclohexane contains:

$6+12=18\text{atoms}$

Therefore, in $2$ moles of cyclohexane, moles of atoms are:

$2\times 18=36\text{moles of atoms}$

(B) 684 g of sucrose
Sucrose has formula:

$\mathrm{C}_{12}\mathrm{H}_{22}\mathrm{O}_{11}$

Total atoms in one molecule:

$12+22+11=45$

Molar mass of sucrose:

$12\times 12+22\times 1+11\times 16$

$=144+22+176=342\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Given mass $=684$ g, so moles of sucrose:

$\frac{684}{342}=2\text{mol}$

Hence, moles of atoms:

$2\times 45=90\text{moles of atoms}$

(C) 90.8 L of dihydrogen at STP
At STP, $1$ mole of any gas occupies $22.4$ L.

So moles of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$:

$\frac{90.8}{22.4}\approx 4.05\text{mol}$

Each molecule of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ has $2$ atoms.

Therefore, moles of atoms:

$4.05\times 2=8.10\text{moles of atoms}$

Comparison

(A) $=36$ moles of atoms

(B) $=90$ moles of atoms

(C) $=8.10$ moles of atoms

So the correct order is:

$\mathrm{B}>\mathrm{A}>\mathrm{C}$

Therefore, the correct option is:

$\text{Option D}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
The species having identical radii according to the Bohr's theory are :

A. H (first orbit)

B. $\mathrm{He}^{+}$(first orbit)

C. $\mathrm{He}^{+}$(Second orbit)

D. $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$ (first orbit)

E. $\mathrm{Be}^{3+}$ (Second orbit)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a hydrogen-like species, according to Bohr’s theory, the radius of the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit is

$r_{n}=\frac{n^{2}a_{0}}{Z}$

where:

$n$ = orbit number

$Z$ = atomic number

$a_{0}$ = Bohr radius

So, for identical radii, the value of $\dfrac{n^{2}}{Z}$ must be same.

Now check each species:

A. H (first orbit)
For hydrogen, $Z=1$, $n=1$

$r=\frac{1^{2}a_{0}}{1}=a_{0}$

B. $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ (first orbit)
Here, $Z=2$, $n=1$

$r=\frac{1^{2}a_{0}}{2}=\frac{a_{0}}{2}$

C. $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ (second orbit)
Here, $Z=2$, $n=2$

$r=\frac{2^{2}a_{0}}{2}=\frac{4a_{0}}{2}=2a_{0}$

D. $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$ (first orbit)
Here, $Z=3$, $n=1$

$r=\frac{1^{2}a_{0}}{3}=\frac{a_{0}}{3}$

E. $\mathrm{Be}^{3+}$ (second orbit)
Here, $Z=4$, $n=2$

$r=\frac{2^{2}a_{0}}{4}=\frac{4a_{0}}{4}=a_{0}$

Now compare:

A: $a_{0}$

B: $\dfrac{a_{0}}{2}$

C: $2a_{0}$

D: $\dfrac{a_{0}}{3}$

E: $a_{0}$

So, the identical radii are for A and E.

Therefore, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option B: A and E Only}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
At $27^{\circ }\mathrm{C},0.1\mathrm{M},1\mathrm{L}\mathrm{K}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$ aqueous solution and $0.1\mathrm{M},1\mathrm{L}\mathrm{FeCl}_{3}$ aqueous solution are placed in a container separated by a semi permeable membrane AB . Assume complete dissociation of both the solutes. Which of the following statement is correct?

[IMG]
options: Blue color is formed on both sides.
Ionic solutes in aqueous solution can pass through semi-permeable membrane.
Solution on side ' y ' is hypotonic.
To cause the reverse flow of solvent during osmosis, external pressure (any value) should be applied to side ' $x$ '.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
(A) A semi-permeable membrane (SPM) allows only solvent molecules (water) to pass through it. It does not allow ions to pass.

So, the solute ions from the two sides cannot come together. Therefore, no blue colour (due to mixing of ions) will appear on either side.

(B) Because ions cannot cross the SPM, only solvent molecules can move from one side to the other depending on osmotic pressure.

(C) A hypotonic solution is the one which has lower osmotic pressure (lower “effective” concentration of solute particles).

We use the NCERT relation for osmotic pressure:

As osmotic pressure $(π)=iCRT$

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{K}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]⟶4\mathrm{K}^{+}+\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}^{-4}(\because i=5) \\ \mathrm{FeCl}_{3}⟶\mathrm{Fe}^{+3}+3\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(\because i=4) \\ \text{for side}x:π=5\mathrm{CRT}=0.5\mathrm{RT}(\because c=0.1\mathrm{m}) \\ \, ~\quad \qquad y:π=0.4RT(\because c=0.1\mathrm{m}) \end{array}$

effective concentration of $x=i\times C=0.5\mathrm{M}$

$y=i\times C=0.4\mathrm{m}$

Since, effective concentration of $y$ is less than $x$. Hence, $y$ is hypotonic.

(D) In reverse osmosis, pressure is applied on the side having higher osmotic pressure (here, side $x$). But this applied external pressure must be greater than the osmotic pressure difference between the two sides.

i.e. P applied > $(π_{x}-π_{y})$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text: 20 mL of a solution of acetic acid required 28.4 mL of 0.1 M NaOH for its neutralization. A solution (X) was prepared by mixing 20 mL of the above acetic acid and 14.2 mL of 0.1 M NaOH solution. What is the pH of the solution $(\mathrm{X})$ ? $(\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{a}}$ value of acetic acid is 4.75).
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For neutralization of acetic acid:

$\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{NaOH}\to \mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COONa}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

The reaction is in the ratio $1:1$.

Given that $20\text{mL}$ of acetic acid requires $28.4\text{mL}$ of $0.1\text{M}$ NaOH for complete neutralization.

So, moles of acetic acid in $20\text{mL}$ are:

$n(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH})=0.1\times \frac{28.4}{1000}=2.84\times 10^{-3}\text{mol}$

Now solution $X$ is prepared by mixing:

$20\text{mL}$ acetic acid

$14.2\text{mL}$ of $0.1\text{M}$ NaOH

Moles of NaOH added:

$n(\mathrm{NaOH})=0.1\times \frac{14.2}{1000}=1.42\times 10^{-3}\text{mol}$

NaOH will neutralize equal moles of acetic acid.

Initial moles of acetic acid:

$2.84\times 10^{-3}$

Moles neutralized:

$1.42\times 10^{-3}$

Moles of acetic acid left:

$2.84\times 10^{-3}-1.42\times 10^{-3}=1.42\times 10^{-3}$

Moles of acetate formed:

$1.42\times 10^{-3}$

So after mixing, we have:

acetic acid = $1.42\times 10^{-3}\text{mol}$

acetate ion = $1.42\times 10^{-3}\text{mol}$

This is a buffer solution where:

$[\text{salt}]=[\text{acid}]$

Using Henderson–Hasselbalch equation:

$\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_{a}+\log \frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$

Since both are equal,

$\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}=1\Rightarrow \log 1=0$

Therefore,

$\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_{a}=4.75$

So, the correct answer is:

$4.75$

Option B.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
$\text{Match the LIST-I with LIST-II}$

  

    List-I
Reaction

    List-II
Mechanism

  

  

    A.

    Williamson Synthesis

    I.

    Electrophilic addition

  

  

    B.

    Friedel Craft Reaction

    II.

    Free radical substitution

  

  

    C.

    Bromination of vinyl benzene

    III.

    Nucleophilic substitution

  

  

    D.

    Chlorination of toluene in light

    IV.

    Electrophilic substitution

  

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A. Williamson Synthesis
In Williamson ether synthesis, an alkoxide ion attacks an alkyl halide and replaces the halogen.

So, it proceeds by nucleophilic substitution.

$A\to III$

B. Friedel Craft Reaction
Friedel-Crafts reaction in benzene involves attack by an electrophile on the aromatic ring.

So, it is electrophilic substitution.

$B\to IV$

C. Bromination of vinyl benzene
Vinyl benzene is styrene, having a double bond. Bromine adds across the double bond.

This is electrophilic addition.

$C\to I$

D. Chlorination of toluene in light
In presence of light, chlorination of toluene occurs at the side chain by a radical pathway.

So, it is free radical substitution.

$D\to II$

Therefore, the correct matching is:

$A-III,B-IV,C-I,D-II$

So, the correct option is:

$\text{Option C}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text: The $1^{\text{st}}$ ionization enthalpy for Mg is $+737\mathrm{kJ}/\mathrm{mol}$. The most probable estimated value of the $2^{\text{nd}}$ ionization enthalpy of Mg is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For magnesium, the electronic configuration is

$\mathrm{Mg}=1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}$

The first ionization enthalpy corresponds to:

$\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{g})\to \mathrm{Mg}^{+}(\mathrm{g})+e^{-}$

This is given as

$\Delta _{i}H_{1}=+737\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Now the second ionization enthalpy corresponds to removing one more electron from $\mathrm{Mg}^{+}$:

$\mathrm{Mg}^{+}(\mathrm{g})\to \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(\mathrm{g})+e^{-}$

After losing one electron, $\mathrm{Mg}^{+}$ has configuration

$1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{1}$

The second electron is still being removed from the same outermost shell, but now from a positively charged ion. So this electron is held more strongly than in neutral Mg.

Hence:

second ionization enthalpy must be greater than first ionization enthalpy,

ionization enthalpy is always positive.

So options with negative values are impossible, and $+590\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ is less than the first ionization enthalpy, so it is also not possible.

Therefore, the most probable value is

$+1450\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

So, the correct option is C.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
The electronegativity of a group 13 element ' E ' is same as that of Ge (on Pauling scale and upto one decimal point). The CORRECT statements about $\mathrm{E}^{3+}$ are

A. It can act as a reducing agent.

B. It can act as an oxidizing agent.

C. $\mathrm{E}^{3+}$ is more stable than $\mathrm{E}^{+}$.

D. The standard electrode potential value for $\mathrm{E}^{3+}/\mathrm{E}$ is positive.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the group 13 element $E$, we are told that its electronegativity is same as that of Ge.

In group 13, the element whose electronegativity is nearly equal to Ge is thallium, Tl.

So, here

$E=\mathrm{Tl}$

and therefore

$E^{3+}=\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$

Now let us examine the statements one by one.

Important concept: Inert pair effect
In group 13, due to inert pair effect, the outer $ns^{2}$ electrons are less available for bonding in heavier elements.

So for Tl:

$+1$ oxidation state is more stable

$+3$ oxidation state is less stable

Thus, $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$ tends to gain electrons and get reduced to $\mathrm{Tl}^{+}$.

Statement A: It can act as a reducing agent.
A reducing agent causes reduction of another species and itself gets oxidized.

But $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$ is already in a high oxidation state and tends to get reduced, not oxidized further.

So, $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$ does not act as a reducing agent.

Therefore, A is false.

Statement B: It can act as an oxidizing agent.
Since $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$ is less stable and readily gets reduced to $\mathrm{Tl}^{+}$, it can oxidize other substances.

Hence, $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$ acts as an oxidizing agent.

Therefore, B is true.

Statement C: $E^{3+}$ is more stable than $E^{+}$.
For Tl, because of inert pair effect:

$\mathrm{Tl}^{+}\text{is more stable than}\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$

So this statement is false.

Therefore, C is false.

Statement D: The standard electrode potential value for $E^{3+}/E$ is positive.
For thallium, the standard reduction potential for

$\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}+3e^{-}\to \mathrm{Tl}$

is positive.

This is because $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$ is readily reduced.

So, D is true.

Thus, the correct statements are:

$B\text{and}D\text{only}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option C}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
Pairs of elements with the same number of electrons in their respective 4f orbital are

[Atomic number. Eu-63, Gd-64, Dy-66, Ho-67, Tm-69, Yb-70, Lu-71, Hf-72]

A. (Eu and Gd)

B. (Dy and Ho)

C. ( Yb and Hf )

D. ( Lu and Tm)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We need to compare the number of electrons present in the $4f$ orbital for each given element.

For lanthanoids, we write the electronic configurations and count the electrons in $4f$.

Given elements:

$\text{Eu}(63)=[Xe]4f^{7}6s^{2}$

$\text{Gd}(64)=[Xe]4f^{7}5d^{1}6s^{2}$

$\text{Dy}(66)=[Xe]4f^{10}6s^{2}$

$\text{Ho}(67)=[Xe]4f^{11}6s^{2}$

$\text{Tm}(69)=[Xe]4f^{13}6s^{2}$

$\text{Yb}(70)=[Xe]4f^{14}6s^{2}$

$\text{Lu}(71)=[Xe]4f^{14}5d^{1}6s^{2}$

$\text{Hf}(72)=[Xe]4f^{14}5d^{2}6s^{2}$

Now check each pair:

A. Eu and Gd

Eu has $4f^{7}$

Gd has $4f^{7}$

So, same number of $4f$ electrons. This is correct.

B. Dy and Ho

Dy has $4f^{10}$

Ho has $4f^{11}$

Not same. This is incorrect.

C. Yb and Hf

Yb has $4f^{14}$

Hf has $4f^{14}$

Same number of $4f$ electrons. This is correct.

D. Lu and Tm

Lu has $4f^{14}$

Tm has $4f^{13}$

Not same. This is incorrect.

So the correct pairs are:

$A\text{and}C$

Hence, the correct option is:

$\text{Option D}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text: Consider the metal complexes $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{en})_{3}]^{2+}(\mathrm{A}),[\mathrm{NiCl}_{4}]^{2-}(\mathrm{B})$ and $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}]^{2+}(\mathrm{C})$. Choose the CORRECT option by considering the number of unpaired electrons present in (A), (B) and (C) respectively and the order of frequency of absorption.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For all the three complexes, the metal ion is $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$.

The electronic configuration of Ni is

$\mathrm{Ni}:[Ar]3d^{8}4s^{2}$

So,

$\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{8}$

Now let us examine each complex.

1. Complex $(A)=[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{en})_{3}]^{2+}$
Here, $\mathrm{en}$ is ethane-1,2-diamine, a neutral bidentate ligand.

Coordination number $=6$

Geometry $=$ octahedral

For an octahedral $d^{8}$ configuration, the arrangement is:

$t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{2}$

This gives 2 unpaired electrons.

So, for $(A)$:

$\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$

2. Complex $(B)=[\mathrm{NiCl}_{4}]^{2-}$

Coordination number $=4$

Since $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ is a weak ligand, this complex is tetrahedral.

For tetrahedral $d^{8}$, the splitting is small, and the electrons remain high spin.

Hence, it has 2 unpaired electrons.

So, for $(B)$:

$\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$

3. Complex $(C)=[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$

Coordination number $=6$

Geometry $=$ octahedral

Again, for octahedral $d^{8}$:

$t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{2}$

So it also has 2 unpaired electrons.

Thus, for $(C)$:

$\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$

Frequency of absorption
The frequency of absorbed light depends on crystal field splitting:

$\Delta \propto ν$

Greater the splitting, greater the frequency of absorption.

Now compare ligand strengths:

$\mathrm{en}>\mathrm{NH}_{3}>\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$

Also, tetrahedral complexes have smaller splitting than octahedral complexes.

So,

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{en})_{3}]^{2+}$ has the highest $\Delta$

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ has next

$[\mathrm{NiCl}_{4}]^{2-}$ has the least

Therefore, order of frequency of absorption is:

$(A)>(C)>(B)$

Hence the correct option is:

$\text{Option A}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
Consider $|x|$ is the difference in oxidation states of Mn in highest manganese fluoride and highest manganese oxide. The ions with $|x|$ number of unpaired electrons from the following are :

A. $\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$

B. $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$

C. $\mathrm{V}^{2+}$

D. $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$

E. $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The highest fluoride of manganese is $\mathrm{MnF}{}_{4}$ (Mn = +4), while the highest oxide is $\mathrm{Mn}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{7}$ (Mn = +7), because oxygen stabilises higher oxidation states by multiple bonding. So $|x|=7-4=3$.

Unpaired electrons: $\mathrm{Sc}{}^{3+}$ $3d^{0}$, 0; $\mathrm{Zn}{}^{2+}$ $3d^{10}$, 0; $\mathrm{V}{}^{2+}$ $3d^{3}$, 3; $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{2+}$ $3d^{6}$, 4; $\mathrm{Co}{}^{2+}$ $3d^{7}$, 3.

Only C ($\mathrm{V}{}^{2+}$) and E ($\mathrm{Co}{}^{2+}$) have 3 unpaired electrons.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
Consider the given graph showing variation of reactant concentration with time.

Three different reactions were started with identical initial concentration of reactants. Which of the following statement is correct?

[IMG]
options: The order of all the three reactions is same.
The rate constant of reaction 3 is larger than the rate constant of reaction 2 if the order of reaction is same for both.
The SI unit of rate constant of reaction 1 is $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.
Thermal decomposition of HI on gold surface is an example of reaction 2 .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Curve 1 is a straight line, $[\mathrm{R}]=[\mathrm{R}]_{0}-kt$, so reaction 1 is zero order; curves 2 and 3 are exponential decays. The three reactions do not all have the same order, so (A) is wrong.

For a given order, the concentration left at time $t$ from the same $[\mathrm{R}]_{0}$ depends only on the product $kt$ and is smaller for a larger $k$ (for first order, $[\mathrm{R}]=[\mathrm{R}]_{0}e^{-kt}$). At every instant curve 3 lies below curve 2, so $k_{3}>k_{2}$ and (B) is correct.

The rate constant of a zero-order reaction has units of concentration per time, $\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$, not $\text{s}^{-1}$, so (C) is wrong.

Thermal decomposition of $\mathrm{HI}$ on a gold surface is zero order (rate $=k$), so it is an example of reaction 1, not reaction 2; (D) is wrong.

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

[IMG]

Compound $(\mathrm{X})$ is subjected to the sequence of reactions as shown above. Molar mass of the major product $(\mathrm{Y})$ formed is $____$ $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$.

(Given molar mass in $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\mathrm{C}:12,\mathrm{H}:1,\mathrm{O}:16$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{Br}{}_{2}$ in $\mathrm{CHCl}{}_{3}$ adds to the vinyl group of styrene (X) to give $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{CHBrCH}{}_{2}\mathrm{Br}$.

Excess $\mathrm{NaNH}{}_{2}$ removes two molecules of $\mathrm{HBr}$ to give phenylacetylene, and the extra $\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}{}^{-}$ deprotonates this terminal alkyne to the acetylide $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{C}{}^{-}$.

$\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{I}$ alkylates the acetylide ($\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$) to give 1-phenylpropyne, $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{CCH}{}_{3}$.

$\mathrm{Na}$ in liquid $\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}$ reduces the internal alkyne to the trans-alkene, so Y is (E)-1-phenylprop-1-ene, $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CHCH}{}_{3}$, $\mathrm{C}{}_{9}\mathrm{H}{}_{10}$.

$M(\mathrm{C}{}_{9}\mathrm{H}{}_{10})=9(12)+10(1)=118\text{g mol}^{-1}$

text: The strongest conjugate acid will result from :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A weaker base gives a stronger conjugate acid, so the strongest conjugate acid comes from the least basic amine.

In (B) $p$-anisidine the $-\mathrm{OCH}{}_{3}$ group releases electrons into the ring by $+M$ effect, raising the electron density on the $-\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$ nitrogen: most basic.

In (D) $p$-toluidine the $-\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ group releases electrons by $+I$ effect and hyperconjugation, a weaker push than the $+M$ effect of $-\mathrm{OCH}{}_{3}$.

In (A) aniline the nitrogen lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring, with no substituent help.

In (C) $p$-nitroaniline the $-\mathrm{NO}{}_{2}$ group withdraws electrons by $-M$ and $-I$ effects, and the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised through the ring onto the nitro group: least basic.

Basicity: (B) > (D) > (A) > (C), with p$K_{a}$ of the anilinium ions about 5.3, 5.1, 4.6 and 1.0. Conjugate acid strength is the reverse, (C) > (A) > (D) > (B), so the $p$-nitroanilinium ion is the strongest conjugate acid.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: A D-aldotetrose on oxidation with concentrated $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ resulted in optically inactive dicarboxylic acid. The structure of the D-aldotetrose is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Concentrated $\mathrm{HNO}{}_{3}$ oxidises both the CHO and the $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$ groups of an aldotetrose to COOH, giving tartaric acid, $\mathrm{HOOC}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH})-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH})-\mathrm{COOH}$.

This acid is optically inactive only in its meso form, in which the two OH groups lie on the same side of the Fischer projection and the molecule has a plane of symmetry. The tetrose must therefore be erythrose; threose, with the two OH groups on opposite sides as in (B) and (D), gives optically active tartaric acid.

A D-sugar has the OH on the stereocentre next to $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$ on the right. Structure (C) has both OH groups on the right (D-erythrose), whereas (A) has both on the left (L-erythrose).


[IMG]

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: Among $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+},\mathrm{Pb}^{2+},\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$, identify the one that gets precipitated out while passing $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ in presence of $\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}$ as group reagent. The highest possible oxidation state of the corresponding metal is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In cation analysis, $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ in the presence of $\mathrm{NH}{}_{4}\mathrm{OH}$ (with $\mathrm{NH}{}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}$) is the group reagent of group IV, which precipitates $\mathrm{Zn}{}^{2+}$, $\mathrm{Mn}{}^{2+}$, $\mathrm{Co}{}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Ni}{}^{2+}$ as sulphides.

$\mathrm{Pb}{}^{2+}$ (partly removed in group I as $\mathrm{PbCl}{}_{2}$) and $\mathrm{Cu}{}^{2+}$ are precipitated earlier, in group II, as $\mathrm{PbS}$ and $\mathrm{CuS}$ by $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ in dilute $\mathrm{HCl}$; $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{3+}$ is precipitated in group III as $\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{OH}){}_{3}$ by $\mathrm{NH}{}_{4}\mathrm{OH}$ in the presence of $\mathrm{NH}{}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}$.

So the ion precipitated by this group reagent is $\mathrm{Mn}{}^{2+}$, as buff-coloured $\mathrm{MnS}$.

Manganese ($[\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{2}$) can use all seven valence electrons, so its highest oxidation state is +7, as in $\mathrm{KMnO}{}_{4}$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

solution.body:
Tollen’s test: This test helps to identify aldehydes. When an aldehyde reacts with Tollen’s reagent, a silver mirror is formed on the inner walls of the test tube.

Hinsberg’s reagent test: This test is used to distinguish different types of amines. The reaction with benzene sulphonyl chloride (Hinsberg’s reagent) gives different products for primary, secondary, and tertiary amines.

Lucas test: This test is used to identify alcohols. Alcohols react with Lucas reagent (a mixture of concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl₂), forming turbidity depending on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary, or tertiary.

Phthalein dye test: This test is used to detect phenols. Phenols react with phthalic anhydride in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to form coloured phthalein dyes.

text:
If 3.365 g of ethanol $(\mathrm{l})$ is burnt completely in a bomb calorimeter at 298.15 K , the heat produced is 99.472 kJ . The $|\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{f}}{}^{\circ }|$ of ethanol at 298.15 K is

$____$ $\times 10^{2}\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$. (Nearest integer)

Given: Standard enthalpy for combustion of graphite $=-393.5\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Standard enthalpy of formation of water $(\mathrm{l})=-285.8\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Molar mass in $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ of $\mathrm{C},\mathrm{H},\mathrm{O}$ are 12,1 and 16 respectively
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For complete combustion of ethanol,

$\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{OH}(\mathrm{l})+3\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\to 2\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+3\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$

First, calculate moles of ethanol burnt:

Molar mass of ethanol, $\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{OH}$:

$2(12)+6(1)+16=46\mathrm{g}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

So, moles of ethanol:

$n=\frac{3.365}{46}=0.07315\mathrm{mol}$

Given heat produced for $0.07315$ mol ethanol is $99.472$ kJ.

Hence, molar heat of combustion at constant volume:

$\Delta U_{\text{comb}}=\frac{-99.472}{0.07315}$

$\Delta U_{\text{comb}}\approx -1359.8\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Now use the relation:

$\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_{g}RT$

Here, in the combustion reaction:

Gaseous reactants = $3$ mol $\mathrm{O}_{2}$

Gaseous products = $2$ mol $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$

So,

$\Delta n_{g}=2-3=-1$

Thus,

$\Delta H_{\text{comb}}=\Delta U_{\text{comb}}+(-1)RT$

At $298.15$ K,

$RT=\frac{8.314\times 298.15}{1000}\approx 2.478\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Therefore,

$\Delta H_{\text{comb}}=-1359.8-2.478=-1362.3\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Now apply Hess's law:

$\Delta H_{\text{comb}}^{\circ }=\left [2\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{CO}_{2})+3\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})\right ]-\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{OH})$

Given:

$\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{CO}_{2})=-393.5\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

$\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}))=-285.8\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

So,

$-1362.3=[2(-393.5)+3(-285.8)]-\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{ethanol})$

$-1362.3=[-787.0-857.4]-\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{ethanol})$

$-1362.3=-1644.4-\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{ethanol})$

$\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }(\mathrm{ethanol})=-1644.4+1362.3=-282.1\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Therefore,

$\left |\Delta H_{f}^{\circ }\right |=282.1\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}=2.821\times 10^{2}\mathrm{kJ}\quad \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Nearest integer:

$3$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
For the following reaction at $50^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ and at 2 atm pressure,

$2\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}(\mathrm{g})⇌2\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$

$\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}$ is $50%$ dissociated.

The magnitude of standard free energy change at this temperature is $x$.

$x=$ $____$ $\mathrm{J}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ [Nearest integer].

Given : $\mathrm{R}=8.314\mathrm{J}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\mathrm{K}^{-1},\log 2=0.30,\log 3=0.48,\ln 10=2.303$, ${}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}+273=\mathrm{K}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Take 1 mol of $\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{5}$. At 50% dissociation, 0.5 mol of $\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{5}$ reacts and forms 0.5 mol of $\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}$ and 0.25 mol of $\mathrm{O}{}_{2}$.

At equilibrium $n(\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{5})=0.5$, $n(\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4})=0.5$ and $n(\mathrm{O}{}_{2})=0.25$, a total of 1.25 mol.

At a total pressure of 2 atm, $p_{\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{5}}=\dfrac{0.5}{1.25}\times 2=0.8\text{atm}$, $p_{\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}}=0.8\text{atm}$ and $p_{\mathrm{O}{}_{2}}=\dfrac{0.25}{1.25}\times 2=0.4\text{atm}$.

$K_{p}=\dfrac{p_{\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}}^{2}p_{\mathrm{O}{}_{2}}}{p_{\mathrm{N}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{5}}^{2}}=\dfrac{(0.8)^{2}(0.4)}{(0.8)^{2}}=0.4$

$\log 0.4=2\log 2-1=0.60-1=-0.40$, so $\ln 0.4=2.303\times (-0.40)=-0.9212$.

At $T=50+273=323\text{K}$:

$\Delta G^{\circ }=-RT\ln K_{p}=-8.314\times 323\times (-0.9212)=+2473.8\text{J mol}^{-1}$

The magnitude, to the nearest integer, is $2474\text{J mol}^{-1}$.

Hence, the answer is 2474.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
An electrochemical cell consists of the following two redox couples, $\mathrm{M}^{x+}(\mathrm{aq})/\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{s})\left [\mathrm{E}_{\text{red}}^{\Theta }=+0.15\mathrm{V}\right ]$ and $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})/\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{s})\left [\mathrm{E}_{\text{red}}^{\Theta }=-0.036\mathrm{V}\right ]$. The cell EMF $\left (\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}\right )$ is recorded to be 0.2057 V . If the reaction quotient of the electrochemical reaction is found to be $10^{-2}$, then the value of $x$ is

$____$ .(Nearest integer)

[Given : M is a p-block metal and $\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059\mathrm{V}$ ]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the cell, the two reduction potentials are:

$\mathrm{M}^{x+}+xe^{-}\to \mathrm{M}(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ }=+0.15\text{V}$

and

$\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+3e^{-}\to \mathrm{Fe}(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ }=-0.036\text{V}$

Since the reduction potential of $\mathrm{M}^{x+}/\mathrm{M}$ is greater, it will act as the cathode.

So,

Cathode: $\mathrm{M}^{x+}+xe^{-}\to \mathrm{M}(s)$

Anode: $\mathrm{Fe}(s)\to \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+3e^{-}$

Hence,

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ }-E_{\text{anode}}^{\circ }=0.15-(-0.036)=0.186\text{V}$

Now use the Nernst equation:

$E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }-\frac{0.059}{n}\log Q$

Given:

$E_{\text{cell}}=0.2057\text{V},Q=10^{-2}$

Since $\log 10^{-2}=-2$,

$0.2057=0.186-\frac{0.059}{n}(-2)$

$0.2057=0.186+\frac{0.118}{n}$

$0.2057-0.186=\frac{0.118}{n}$

$0.0197=\frac{0.118}{n}$

$n=\frac{0.118}{0.0197}\approx 5.99\approx 6$

So the number of electrons transferred in the balanced cell reaction is

$n=6$

Now, for balancing electrons:

Oxidation of iron gives $3$ electrons

Reduction of $\mathrm{M}^{x+}$ consumes $x$ electrons

Therefore, total electrons transferred in the balanced equation will be $\mathrm{LCM}(3,x)$.

Given this is $6$, we get:

$\mathrm{LCM}(3,x)=6$

Possible values of $x$ are $2$ or $6$.

Now it is given that $\mathrm{M}$ is a p-block metal. Common p-block metals generally form ions like $2^{+}$, $3^{+}$, $4^{+}$, etc. Among the possible values, the most suitable is

$x=2$

So, the nearest integer value of $x$ is

$2$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text:
$\text{For a first order reaction}\mathrm{A}\to \mathrm{B}$

$\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{t}/\min  & [\mathrm{A}]/\mathrm{M} \\ 0 & 0.6500 \\ x & 0.0650 \\ 20 & 0.00065 \end{array}$

$x=$ $____$ min. (Nearest integer)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a first order reaction, the integrated rate law is

$k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log \frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}}$

We use the data at $t=20$ min:

Initial concentration, $[A]_{0}=0.6500\text{M}$

Concentration at $20$ min, $[A]_{20}=0.00065\text{M}$

So,

$k=\frac{2.303}{20}\log \frac{0.6500}{0.00065}$

Now,

$\frac{0.6500}{0.00065}=1000$

and

$\log 1000=3$

Therefore,

$k=\frac{2.303}{20}\times 3$

$k=\frac{6.909}{20}$

$k=0.34545\text{\min }^{-1}$

Now we use the concentration at time $x$:

$[A]_{x}=0.0650\text{M}$

Again,

$k=\frac{2.303}{x}\log \frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{x}}$

$0.34545=\frac{2.303}{x}\log \frac{0.6500}{0.0650}$

Now,

$\frac{0.6500}{0.0650}=10$

and

$\log 10=1$

So,

$0.34545=\frac{2.303}{x}$

Hence,

$x=\frac{2.303}{0.34545}$

$x\approx 6.67\text{\min }$

Nearest integer:

$7\text{\min }$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift

text: In sulphur estimation, $2.0\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{mol}$ of an organic compound $(\mathrm{X})$ (molar mass $76\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ) gave 0.4813 g of barium sulphate (molar mass $233\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ). The percentage of sulphur in the compound $(\mathrm{X})$ is $____$ $\times 10^{-1}%$ (Nearest integer)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We are given the number of moles and the molar mass of compound (X). We can find its total mass using the formula:

$\text{Mass}=\text{Moles}\times \text{Molar Mass}$

$\text{Mass of compound (X)}=2.0\times 10^{-3}\text{mol}\times 76\text{g mol}^{-1}$

$\text{Mass of compound (X)}=152\times 10^{-3}\text{g}=0.152\text{g}$

In the Carius method, the sulphur in the organic compound is quantitatively converted into barium sulphate ($\mathrm{BaSO}_{4}$). 

According to the molar masses:

$1\text{mole of}\mathrm{BaSO}_{4}(233\text{g})\text{contains}1\text{mole of Sulphur}(32\text{g})$.

Therefore, the mass of sulphur in $0.4813\text{g}$ of $\mathrm{BaSO}_{4}$ is:

$\text{Mass of Sulphur}=\frac{32}{233}\times \text{Mass of}\mathrm{BaSO}_{4}$

$\text{Mass of Sulphur}=\frac{32}{233}\times 0.4813\text{g}$

$%\text{of Sulphur}=\frac{\text{Mass of Sulphur}}{\text{Total mass of compound (X)}}\times 100$

Substitute the values we found in Steps 1 and 2:

$%\text{of Sulphur}=\left (\frac{\frac{32}{233}\times 0.4813}{0.152}\right )\times 100$

$%\text{of Sulphur}=\frac{32\times 0.4813\times 100}{233\times 0.152}$

$%\text{of Sulphur}=\frac{1540.16}{35.416}$

$%\text{of Sulphur}\approx 43.4877%$

We need to express the answer in the form of $____\times 10^{-1}%$. Let us rewrite our percentage:

$43.4877%=434.877\times 10^{-1}%$

When we round $434.877$ to the nearest integer, we get $435$.

The percentage of sulphur in the compound (X) is 435 $\times 10^{-1}%$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Evening Shift
